blocks.text: The language identification model was trained for 2 epochs on 130124 RMS training units (9502124 tokens). It passes all 7 of 7 checks: every language is at or above the 90% floor, and none has regressed below the base. Macro accuracy rose by 68.2 points. The model is recorded as admitted.

The result is strong but uneven in headroom. Kikamba (91.3%) and Luhya (93.5%) are closest to the floor, and Luhya abstains on 4.2% of items. The next improvement should therefore be targeted data for those two languages, followed by a review of abstention behaviour.
The held-out results have been inspected, so they cannot count as independent final acceptance for any further recipe choice. This paper covers the retained measurements from this run only.

All 7 of 7 languages are at or above the 90% floor and none falls below the base. The largest gains came where the base was weakest. Kikamba rose from 0.0% to 91.3%, Ekegusii from 1.1% to 98.2%, and Luhya from 4.3% to 93.5%. Gikuyu reached 99.2% from 24.5%, and Kalenjin 99.7% from 11.9%.

Kiswahili is the exception in kind. Its base already scored 98.4%, and the model reaches 99.0%, so the gain there is small. Kikamba and Luhya have the thinnest margins over the floor, and a modest drop on fresh material could take either below it. That is the main reason to prioritise them.

sections.heading: Every language clears the floor; two have little headroom

blocks.text: Training used 130124 units and 9502124 tokens of RMS transcripts. Scoring used a sealed held-out set of 2800 units. The record does not split that set by language, so the uncertainty around each per-language figure cannot be stated. This matters most for Kikamba and Luhya, where margins are thin.

The run took 0.8 GPU-hours, or 49 minutes on one GPU. Compute is therefore not the constraint on iteration. Abstention varies from 0.5% for Gikuyu to 4.8% for Kiswahili, with Luhya at 4.2% and Kikamba at 1.8%. The record does not say whether abstentions count as errors in the accuracy figures.

sections.heading: Data, compute and abstention behind the result

blocks.text: First, expand Kikamba and Luhya training and held-out data, since these have the least headroom over the 90% floor. Second, confirm how abstention is scored, then review it for Luhya (4.2%) and Kiswahili (4.8%). Changing a threshold before knowing this could move accuracy without improving the model.

Third, commission fresh, independently labelled sealed material before selecting another recipe, because the 2800 held-out units have been inspected. Fourth, change one thing per run. At 0.8 GPU-hours a run, this is affordable and lets any change in Kikamba or Luhya be attributed to its cause.

sections.heading: What to do first, and why

blocks.text: Performance outside the measured languages and the sealed set is not established; an independently designed evaluation would close that gap. Independent final acceptance is not possible after further recipe selection on inspected results, and needs fresh, sealed, independently labelled material.

No new production plan is linked to this historical run, so lineage from objective to production is incomplete. Closing it needs an explicitly compiled, evidence-linked objective, never a backdated assumption. Serving is a separate operation: the full adapter is served and the pruned adapter is admitted but not served. The record carries no evidence on privacy handling of the transcripts.
